title: Spectre v1 and the cache side channel
hook: How does speculative execution leak data through the cache in Spectre v1?

scenes.caption: A bounds check is predicted, so the CPU runs the guarded code before the check resolves.
scenes.narration: Speculation lets a CPU run past a branch before it resolves. If the bounds check is slow to resolve, the CPU can execute the body for an out-of-range index, using the predicted direction.

scenes.caption: Attacker trains the predictor with valid x, then passes a malicious out-of-bounds x.
scenes.narration: First the attacker calls the gadget many times with in-bounds indices, training the predictor to expect the check to pass. Then they pass an out-of-bounds index pointing at a secret.

items: 1. Call with valid x many times

scenes.caption: Speculatively, array1[x] reads the secret and its value picks a cache line in array2.
scenes.narration: In the speculative window, the load reads a secret byte beyond the array. That byte, times 512, indexes array2, which pulls exactly one line of array2 into the cache.

scenes.caption: The CPU squashes the results, but the cache line stays: timing reveals the byte.
scenes.narration: The CPU discards the architectural results, but the cache keeps its change. The attacker times a read of each array2 line. The one fast access reveals the secret byte value.

scenes.caption: Mitigate by blocking speculation on the index: lfence or Linux's array_index_nospec().
scenes.narration: Defenses stop the speculative use of the index. Insert an lfence after the check, or clamp the index with the kernel's array_index_nospec macro, so out-of-range values become zero.

takeaway: Spectre v1 turns a mispredicted bounds check into a cache-timing read of out-of-bounds memory, because speculation leaves cache traces.
